posts.title: Asking for a rating once, at the right moment
posts.description: How Exitwise asks for a rating: the store's own card on your third opening, after a win, once. A few openings later, an offer of help. Nothing more.
posts.lede: Every game wants ratings, and most players have met one that wants them too much: a pop-up at launch, a “Do you love us?” question, the same request after every level. Exitwise 1.0.37, out on 7 November, is the first of our games to ask, and we wrote the rule down before we wrote the code. It fits on one line: ask once, at a good moment, with the store's own card, and after that offer help instead of asking again.

sections.title: What counts as an opening
paragraphs: An opening is a cold start that reaches the game's first screen. Switching to another app and coming back doesn't count, so answering a message in the middle of a level never moves the count on. The count lives on your device and nowhere else. It isn't synced to your account, and nothing but the game on that phone reads it.

sections.title: The third opening, after a win
paragraphs: On your third opening, Exitwise waits for a good moment, which in a puzzle game means a level won. Never at launch, never during play, never over an ad. When that moment comes, it calls Google Play's own rating card, the one with the stars that opens over the game, and nothing else.

There's no question of ours before it. That's partly taste and partly the rules. Google's guidelines for the in-app review card forbid asking anything before or while it shows, “Do you like the app?” included, and Apple's App Store guidelines allow only Apple's own prompt. A question that sorts happy players from unhappy ones before showing the card is exactly what those rules are written to stop, and it would make the ratings tell you less.

The store decides whether its card actually appears, because it keeps its own limit on how often one person sees it. So we call it once and never retry. If the third opening has no win in it, or another prompt is already waiting, the game tries on the fourth. After that it never brings it up again.

sections.title: Help on the sixth
paragraphs: On the sixth opening (or the seventh, if the sixth is busy) the game asks something else: “Need help or have an idea?” Open a ticket takes you to our ticket desk, where you can report a bug, ask a question or tell us what you'd like to see, and then follow the answers. Not now closes it for good.

We ask this one ourselves, because no store has a card for it, and because the answer is worth more to us than a star. A rating says how someone felt. A ticket says what went wrong or what's missing, and it reaches the person who can fix it. In the browser there's no store card at all, so the web version of Exitwise makes only the help offer.

sections.title: One prompt per opening
paragraphs: Exitwise already has a few questions of its own. After your third win it invites you to sign in, asks for your birth year if your account needs one, and offers the tutorial. Those always come first. A rating or a help offer that would land in the same opening waits for the next one, so you never get two prompts back to back.

A unit test walks through openings one to eight and checks all of it: the rating on the third (or the fourth), help on the sixth (or the seventh), each once, never two in one opening, and nothing while you play.

sections.title: Always one tap away
paragraphs: A prompt that shows once is easy to miss, so Settings now has two rows that never go away: Rate us, which opens the game's store page, and Help & ideas, which opens the ticket desk. The Rate us row can't open the in-app card, because both stores forbid putting their card behind a button: with the card's own limit, the button would do nothing half the time.
The same rule applies to every game and app we make, so Speedometer Live Wallpaper and Palermo Noir will ask in the same way, in the same order.

posts.title: Exitwise comes to iPhone and iPad
posts.description: Exitwise 1.0.2 is out for iPhone and iPad: the same 600 levels, Sign in with Apple and Restore purchases. Why EU players get the beta for now.
posts.lede: On 7 November Exitwise reached the App Store, for iPhone and iPad. It's the very game Android players and browser players already know, with all 600 levels across its 17 worlds. If you live in the European Union you won't find it in your App Store just yet, though. This post is about what the iPhone version brings, why Europe is waiting, and how to play it there in the meantime.

sections.title: One game, three places
paragraphs: Exitwise is built once, in Unity, and that one project makes the Android app, the iPhone app and the version that runs on this site. The rules of the puzzle sit in a part of the code that knows nothing about phones or browsers, with its own tests, so the iPhone didn't need a port of the game. It needed a new place to run it.

Each level grows from one fixed number, its seed, so level 237 on an iPhone is the same board as level 237 on Android or in a browser, arrow for arrow. That's what makes a per-level leaderboard fair: everyone on it solved the same puzzle.

sections.title: Sign in with Apple
paragraphs: On Apple's devices, the sign-in button is Apple's own. Signing in is optional, and the game plays the same without it. What it gives you is a free VHub account, which keeps your progress safe and gives you one profile across all of our games.

sections.title: Restore purchases
paragraphs: Exitwise is free. If you've bought Remove Ads, that's the kind of purchase that lasts, and Apple asks every app that sells one to offer a way to get it back on a new device. So Settings has Restore purchases: on a new iPhone or iPad, tap it, and Remove Ads comes back without paying again.

sections.title: Why not in the EU yet
paragraphs: Under the EU's Digital Services Act, an app that sells anything has to say who the trader behind it is, and Apple checks those details before the app can appear in any EU storefront. Ours are with Apple and still being checked. Until that's done, Exitwise isn't listed in EU App Stores. An EU visitor to our Exitwise page sees a line under the App Store badge saying so, so nobody taps through to a page that won't open.

sections.title: Playing in the EU meanwhile
paragraphs: There are two ways to play in the EU today. The first is the iPhone beta, through TestFlight, Apple's own app for testing builds: install TestFlight, open the invite link on our Exitwise page, and the game installs like any other. It's the real game, not a demo, and if you sign in, your progress stays with your VHub account whichever version you play.

The second needs nothing at all: Exitwise runs in the browser, on this site, on a phone or a computer. As soon as Apple finishes its check, the App Store version will open in the EU too, and we'll say so on the Exitwise page.

posts.title: One motion for everything that opens
posts.description: Every menu, question and panel in our games, apps and this site opens in 260 ms and closes in 200. Why one shared motion, and the two bugs it fixed.
posts.lede: Click a question in the FAQ on any of our product pages and it opens in about a quarter of a second. Open a menu in Exitwise, a card in Speedometer Live Wallpaper or a panel in VHub, and it moves exactly the same way. That's on purpose. Since early November, everything that expands or drops down, in every game, app and page we make, follows one written spec. This post is about the numbers in it, and why we bothered to write them down.

sections.title: The numbers
paragraphs: Opening takes 260 milliseconds. Closing takes 200, a little faster, because by the time you close something you've made up your mind, and the screen shouldn't keep you waiting. Both use the same curve, a strong ease-out (cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1)): the row covers most of its distance in the first frames and settles gently, so it feels quick without looking abrupt.
While a row grows, what's inside it fades in over the same 260 ms. The chevron beside it turns half a circle with it, and on close it turns back the moment the close begins.

sections.title: Nothing snaps
paragraphs: The rule we care about most is that nothing appears or disappears in a single frame. The text inside a closing row stays drawn until the row has shrunk around it, and the row clips what's inside while it moves. Click a row that's still moving and it turns round from wherever it is, height and fade included, instead of jumping to its end first.

sections.title: One open at a time
paragraphs: Lists of questions keep one answer open at a time. Our first version did that by shutting the open answer instantly when you opened another, and it looked like a glitch: one row animated while the other blinked shut. Now opening a row runs the other row's own close at the same time, so one shrinks as the other grows.

sections.title: The page stays where you left it
paragraphs: The second bug was harder to see. To keep the row you clicked under your pointer, an early version nudged the page's scroll while the rows changed height. It worked, and it felt wrong: you opened an answer and the page drifted under you. The spec now says a row never scrolls the page. While rows move, the browser's own scroll anchoring is switched off on whatever is scrolling, and put back a frame after they stop, so the rows below simply move with the heights. Exitwise's web version got this fix on 5 November.

sections.title: Menus and sheets
paragraphs: Menus keep the same timing. A drop-down grows from its button as it fades in. A sheet on a phone rises from the bottom of the screen, and a dialog on a wide screen rises from just below its place. Where a platform already animates its own dialogs both ways, like Android's bottom sheets, we leave them as they are instead of fighting them.

sections.title: Less motion, if you ask for it
paragraphs: If your device is set to reduce motion, nothing slides: rows and menus only fade, in 150 ms opening and 100 ms closing. Screen readers keep a row's open state until its close has finished, so what they announce matches what's on the screen.

sections.title: Why write it down
paragraphs: We build with three very different toolkits: web pages, Unity and Android. Left alone, each would grow its own idea of “smooth”. A spec with numbers in it means each one can be checked against the same thing, and the FAQ on this site is the reference the others are measured against. Speedometer Live Wallpaper 2.0.14 brought it to the app on 4 November, and Exitwise's menus and pop-ups followed the next day.

posts.title: Build your own dashboard: the Speedometer layout builder
posts.description: Speedometer Live Wallpaper now lets you build your own home-screen dashboard from 42 widgets. How snapping, overlaps and readable colours work.

image.alt: Speedometer Live Wallpaper on a tablet: the Grand Tour layout in the Vintage style, with a clock, a power gauge and a compass on walnut, and the weather, a trip computer and the song playing below
image.caption: Grand Tour in the Vintage style on a tablet, one of the layouts we made symmetrical during the review in version 2.0.8.

posts.lede: Until late October, every layout in Speedometer Live Wallpaper was one we had drawn. Version 2.0.7, out on Google Play on 29 October, hands that job to you: a layout builder where you place the gauges yourself, and a market where you can publish what you make. The next two days went into fixing our own layouts, because the builder made their flaws easy to see. This post covers both.

sections.title: One frame for every style
paragraphs: The app has 19 styles, from a walnut dashboard to a jet's head-up display, and a layout has to work in all of them. So every style shares one frame: the screen, minus a thin margin at the sides and top and a deeper one at the bottom, so your row of app icons never sits on top of a gauge. A layout is the same size in every style. You can build it in Vintage, switch to Prism and find every widget where you left it.
A layout holds up to 16 widgets, each kind once. The builder is part of the Android app; on the web you can open any published layout on the try page and see it drawn in any style.

sections.title: Snapping instead of a grid
paragraphs: We tried to avoid a visible grid, because a dashboard isn't a spreadsheet. While you drag a widget, its centre snaps to the middle of the frame or lines up with the centre of another widget, and a thin amber line shows what it caught on. A widget can't be dragged out of the frame. You resize it with a handle, zoom the stage up to four times to place small pieces precisely, and undo or redo any step. With TalkBack on, every widget has move and size actions, so the builder works without dragging at all.

sections.title: Letting widgets overlap
paragraphs: The first version of the builder refused overlaps. A widget dropped onto another turned red and slid to the nearest free space. It looked tidy, and in practice it fought you: real dashboards tuck a small dial into the edge of a big one. So overlaps came back, with Bring to front and Send to back, and a minimum size for each widget so nothing shrinks into an unreadable dot.

Overlaps brought a new problem: grabbing the widget underneath. That is what Lock is for. A locked widget ignores drags and resizes, wears a small padlock, and lets your finger pass through to whatever lies behind it.

sections.title: One widget, nineteen looks
paragraphs: There are 42 kinds of widget: the original 17 and 25 new ones, among them a trip computer, an odometer, a 0–100 widget, a G-force meter, the weather, the moon, your steps, music controls and a second clock. Drawing 42 widgets 19 times by hand wasn't realistic, so each style has a kit. It offers the style's own forms first, cut from its real artwork and never stretched, and then a set of plain forms painted in the style's colours. Every widget has at least one plain form, which is how every style can show every widget.
The builder's Preview in row redraws your layout in any style, including the ones you haven't bought yet.

sections.title: Readable on any background
paragraphs: This was the hardest part. A widget can land anywhere, and the backgrounds run from dark walnut to almost-white glass. In testing, the text of one widget vanished in Rally, and another drew white on nearly white.

We didn't want shadows or boxes behind every number, so the app now measures the tone of each background and dial. A widget keeps its colour only if it stands out at a contrast of at least 3 to 1. If it doesn't, it falls back, in order, to the colour you picked, the style's colour, the dial's own print colour, the display colour, and finally plain white or black. Panels that text can't be read on are recoloured too.

sections.title: Reviewing our own layouts
paragraphs: With a builder in your hands, our built-in layouts became examples, and some were poor ones. An audit of all 52 layouts on 27 October listed 194 problems, big and small, and only two layouts came through clean. Over six review rounds we removed the weakest built-in and ready-made layouts, made Clockmaker, Commute, Road Trip and Grand Tour mirror-symmetric, and added three for tablets and foldables: Grand dash, Wide panel and Fold music. The music card also stopped being one plain box: it is now drawn as each style's own display. All of it shipped in version 2.0.8, released on 30 October.
We also set a rule for ourselves: a layout we make reaches the market only after it has been reviewed by eye.

sections.title: Sharing a layout
paragraphs: Publishing to the market needs a free VHub sign-in. Each published layout gets a six-character code, made only of letters and digits that can't be mistaken for one another, and a link that opens it in the app. Anyone can rate a layout from one to five stars, but only after using it, and never their own. Three open reports hide a layout until we have looked at it. The layouts people have shared are on the site, each drawn by the app itself.

posts.title: One account across our games: what we learned building VHub
posts.description: Exitwise and Speedometer Live Wallpaper share one VHub account. Why accounts live apart from game data, how an app earns XP, and what broke.

image.alt: The 13 VHub rank frames in two rows, each with the level that unlocks it: Wood at level 5, Stone 10, Iron 20, Bronze 30, Silver 45, Gold 60, Platinum 80, Emerald 100, Sapphire 125, Ruby 150, Amethyst 180, Diamond 220 and Mythic 275
image.caption: The 13 rank frames a VHub picture can wear, from Wood at level 5 to Mythic at level 275.

posts.lede: Exitwise started life with accounts of its own: its own name screen, its own picture upload, its own leaderboards. That was fine for one game. With Speedometer Live Wallpaper getting sign-in and more games on the way, it meant a player could end up with a different name, picture and history in every product we make. So in October the accounts moved out of the games and into VHub, one player account for all of them. These are our notes from the move.

sections.title: What VHub keeps, and what each game keeps
paragraphs: The line we drew is simple. Everything about you as a player lives in VHub: your name, your picture, your level and XP, your achievements, your friends and the global leaderboards. Everything about a single game stays with that game: your saved progress, the per-level boards, rooms and custom maps live in the game's own database, filed under the same player ID that VHub gave you.

When you sign in, you sign in to VHub, with your Google account. VHub then hands the game a session for that same ID. No game creates players of its own any more, so there is one of you, not one per product. Change your picture once and every game shows the new one.
Signing in is still optional. Every game and app works without it, and the sign-in prompt can always be skipped.

sections.title: XP for a puzzle game, and for a wallpaper
paragraphs: One level across all our products sounds easy until you try to give XP for a live wallpaper. Exitwise is played: you win levels, finish the daily challenge, publish maps and play matches in rooms, and each of those earns XP, 20 for a level won and 40 for a daily challenge, for example. Speedometer Live Wallpaper isn't played in that sense. It sits on your home screen.

So the wallpaper earns XP for what using it means: a day with the wallpaper on, a style you collect, a layout you build. The daily caps are far apart on purpose: up to 4,000 XP a day from Exitwise, up to 200 from Speedometer, because an evening of hard puzzles and a wallpaper that is simply switched on shouldn't count the same. Every rule is written out on the leaderboards page, because a level means little if nobody can see how it is earned.

sections.title: Your level, worn on your picture
paragraphs: A number next to a name is easy to miss, so since 29 October your picture can wear a frame that shows your rank wherever it appears in Exitwise: on leaderboards, player cards, rooms and match history. There are 13 of them, from a plain wooden ring at level 5 to a winged one at level 275. Each unlocks as your level rises, and you choose which one to wear, or none, with Edit my badge on your VHub profile. Because the picture and the frame both live in VHub, the same frame also shows on the hub, on the vgraphics.gr ranking and beside the Speedometer layouts you share.

sections.title: Moving the players who were already there
paragraphs: Before the switch we had to decide who to bring across from Exitwise. Most of its accounts turned out to be our own: test runs, automated runs that took store screenshots, and guests who opened the game once and never finished a level. Copying all of them would have filled the new leaderboards with robots.

So only real players moved: anyone who had played, signed in, chosen a name or held coins. Their names, pictures, XP and places on the boards came with them. A guest who was left out and comes back simply gets a fresh account. Our own test and robot accounts stayed out, and were deleted only after the list of them had been checked by hand.

sections.title: What broke
paragraphs: On 1 November we noticed that the Exitwise ranking showed none of the new players who had just found the game on Android. The cause was a single name. The Android app asked VHub to sign players in using the full name of the request, and VHub, expecting the short form, didn't recognise it and turned every request from Android away. Android players could still play, but since the update that brought VHub sign-in to Android in late October, none of the new ones had got a VHub account, a row on the boards or their settings synced.

The fix was small: VHub now accepts both forms, and it was live the same evening, with the missing players added to the boards. Since 2 November a new player also reaches the boards the moment they join, and Play Games players show under their gamertag instead of a numbered placeholder. The lasting change is a check that follows a brand-new player from sign-in through to every board and the ranking, and compares what the game recorded with what VHub shows. It runs after every change that touches sign-in, saves, scores or profiles, so we no longer rely on spotting an empty ranking by eye.

sections.title: Leaving
paragraphs: One account also means one clear way out. Each product's profile has Delete my data for that product alone, which keeps your account, name and picture. Delete my VGraphics account removes everything everywhere and signs you out. Both are explained on the deletion page.

posts.title: One clock, not two: reworking the guardian fights in Exitwise
posts.description: Exitwise's guardian levels showed two clocks at once. How we cut them to one, and why the ward's first bump is now free after 300 simulated runs.

image.alt: Exitwise level 160, a guardian fight against Puffcap, before version 1.0.24: a play timer reading 00:28 at the top left and a second clock reading 03:35 in the guardian's strip, above a board of coloured arrows
image.caption: Level 160 against Puffcap before version 1.0.24: play time counting up at the top left, the curse counting down in the guardian's strip.

posts.lede: The last level of every world in Exitwise is a guardian fight. Until the end of October, those fights put two clocks on the screen at the same time. A screenshot of level 160 made the problem plain. This post is about how two clocks became one, and about a lost heart whose real cause wasn't the one we blamed.

sections.title: How a guardian fight works
paragraphs: There are 17 guardians. Bramble waits at the end of the first world, and the last one stands at level 500. You still clear the board by tapping arrows that can fly free, but an arrow that leaves through the top edge also hits the guardian, and the last hit breaks its curse. The curse runs on a clock. Each hit wins a few seconds back, and if the clock runs out, the attempt is lost.

Across part of the top edge sits the ward, a stone shield. Fly an arrow into it and you lose a heart. After a set number of hits, four for most guardians, the ward moves. Later guardians add their own tricks, such as frost that drops numbered ice onto the board, or ink that hides arrows.

sections.title: Two clocks on one screen
paragraphs: Every level in Exitwise has a play timer in the stats row at the top, counting up. Your time decides your stars and your best times. The guardian fights added a second clock inside the guardian's strip, counting down. Both were right, but only one of them could end the fight, and in the screenshot above, the one your eye meets first is the one that can't.

We drew three ways out. In the first, the curse clock takes the play timer's place in the stats row and the strip loses its clock. In the second, the strip keeps its clock and the timer hides. In the third, play time stays and the curse becomes a burning fuse along the strip. We went with the first. The stats row already counts down in Coin Rush, so players know that spot as the one that can run out, and play time still runs underneath, ready for the pause and win cards, so stars and records didn't change.

sections.title: Making one clock say enough
paragraphs: A single clock has to do the work of two, so it changes as time runs low. It turns amber under 30 seconds. Under 10 it turns red and swells a little with every tick you hear. A thin bar under the digits drains as the curse closes in, and every hit throws a small +7 s, or whatever that guardian gives, up above the digits, so you can see the time you just won back. This went out in version 1.0.24 on 28 October.

sections.title: Ice that looked the same
paragraphs: The same update fixed something smaller. Ice dropped by frost and spells picks a number, and it often picked one already on the board: one run of level 220 ended up with three blocks reading 12. Blocks that read the same are hard to tell apart, and three in a row looked like a mistake. New ice now keeps its number at least three apart from the ice already in play.

sections.title: The heart we blamed on the wrong thing
paragraphs: On level 160 we twice lost a heart in a way that felt unfair. Both times an extra arrow from Double-Shot was involved, so we blamed it, and the first fix was aimed at Double-Shot.

Before going further, we measured. We ran the real level 300 times with a simulated player and logged every heart lost to the ward. The real cause was timing. A hit that moves the ward can drop it onto the half of the edge you're working in, and the tap you had already lined up flies straight into it. Those 300 runs had 98 taps like that, most of them right after the player's own hit.

We looked at three answers: warn before the ward moves, stop extra hits from moving it, or let the ward never cost a heart. We chose the warning, in a form that needs no reading ahead: the bump itself is the warning. Since version 1.0.28 on 29 October, your first bump after the ward moves is free. It costs no heart, doesn't count as a mistake or add to the guardian's rage, and your combo keeps going. A short message tells you what happened: “The ward moved! First bump free.” The second bump costs a heart as before.

sections.title: What we took from it
paragraphs: Both changes came from playing our own game on a hard level and paying attention to what felt wrong. In both, the feeling was right and our first explanation wasn't. Now, when a level feels unfair, we measure before we fix.

posts.title: The real Speedometer, running in your browser
posts.description: How the try page runs Speedometer Live Wallpaper's own drawing code in a browser, with Kotlin Multiplatform and Skia, and what a browser can read.
posts.lede: When we added a way to try Speedometer Live Wallpaper online, there were three options: record a video of it, draw a look-alike for the web, or run the app itself. A video can't be tapped, and a look-alike drifts further from the real thing with every update. So the try page runs the app's own drawing code.

sections.title: One renderer, two homes
paragraphs: Every style in the app, from Classic to Harbour, draws with Android's graphics classes: a canvas, paints, paths and gradients. We moved the styles into a Kotlin Multiplatform module that draws through a thin layer with the same class names. On a phone, that layer hands each call straight to Android. In the browser, it hands it to Skia, the graphics library Chrome itself draws with, compiled to WebAssembly.
The styles never know which one they are talking to, so there is no second version of them to keep in step.

sections.title: Proving nothing changed
paragraphs: The app's tests keep reference pictures of the styles in their different states: calibrating, charging, on Wi-Fi, at speed. The rule for the move was strict. Every one of those pictures had to come out byte for byte identical, and a style that shifted by a single pixel meant the move wasn't finished.

sections.title: What a browser can read
paragraphs: On your phone the wallpaper reads the battery, the charger, the network and the processor. In a browser it uses what the browser is willing to share: your clock, in your time zone and with your 12 or 24-hour setting; the battery level and charging, in browsers that share them, such as Chrome; and, if you tap Use my real speed and allow it, your speed from GPS. Your location never leaves your browser.
Everything a browser keeps to itself, like the processor's clock or the phone signal, comes from a short recorded drive, the same one the app plays in its own previews.

sections.title: The one thing it can't do
paragraphs: A web page can't set your wallpaper. That last step belongs to the app, so the page shows a QR code and a Google Play link. Every style you try on the page is in the app; the premium ones are a one-time purchase.

sections.title: Why it was worth it
paragraphs: You can try a premium style live, with its layouts and colours, before you pay for it. And because the page runs the same code, what you see there is what you get on your home screen.

posts.title: Why Exitwise boards stopped being rectangles
posts.description: In October we found Exitwise far too easy by level 60. Part of the fix was the boards themselves: 49 shapes, no slivers and no easy lines.
posts.lede: In October we played Exitwise up to level 60 and had to admit it: it was far too easy. The arrows were fine. A big part of the problem was the boards. A rectangle full of arrows reads quickly: you sweep along the edges, find the arrows pointing out, and the rest falls into place.

sections.title: Shapes change how you read a board
paragraphs: So the boards stopped being mostly rectangles. Exitwise now has 49 board shapes, up from 20: 18 plain ones that fill the screen, from hexagons to spirals, and 31 pictures that hold their own proportions, from a rocket to a castle. Many worlds have pictures of their own, such as Volcano's flame and gem or Glacier's snowflake.
Only the first four levels are plain rectangles, to learn the rules on, and after that only a few. A shaped board has no tidy edge to sweep along, so you read each arrow's path instead.

sections.title: No slivers
paragraphs: Cutting a picture out of a square grid leaves stray single cells along its edges. Every shape is cleaned so that each cell belongs to a solid two-by-two block, and only the largest piece is kept, so a shape reads as a shape.

sections.title: No easy lines
paragraphs: Sometimes the generator left a string of short arrows nose to tail, each starting right in front of the one before and pointing the same way. Each one frees only the next, so the whole string clears in a row of easy taps. A level may now have at most three in a row; one with more is built again from another seed.

sections.title: The same puzzle for everyone
paragraphs: Every level comes from a fixed seed, so every player gets the same board and the leaderboards compare like with like, and every level is tested to be solvable. Every 10th level is a hard level: about one and a half times the size of the levels around it, always a picture, and played at night.
